title: What Happens Inside Your Body When You Drink Coffee?
topic: Caffeine, adenosine signaling, and perceived alertness
style: AFTER THE SIP: tactile ivory ceramic and espresso bronze give way to immersive cyan scientific cinematography. Full-bleed 3D, deliberate lens travel, editorial type, warm-to-cool continuity.

scenes.title: Your brain on coffee
scenes.description: Extreme coffee macro pulls to ceramic cup and rising droplet; typography flips from YOUR BRAIN to ON COFFEE; dive through the liquid.

scenes.title: A molecule enters
scenes.description: Bronze liquid tunnel resolves into a scientifically grounded caffeine molecule; formula appears; camera tracks the molecule into cool fluid.

scenes.title: In the bloodstream
scenes.description: Camera flies between biconcave blood cells inside an organic vessel, following caffeine toward a bright opening.

scenes.title: Blocking adenosine
scenes.description: Detailed human brain orbit becomes a neural close-up, then a stylized seven-helix receptor. Caffeine docks; adenosine cannot occupy the same site.

scenes.title: Less sleepy, more alert
scenes.description: Camera travels through the occupied receptor into a neural forest. Restrained activation and an editorial type transformation explain perceived alertness.

scenes.title: The effect fades
scenes.description: Orbital clock and conceptual decay curve. Molecules leave gradually. Sleep pressure remains. Clearance varies by person.

scenes.title: It masks the signal
scenes.description: Circular scientific motif match-cuts to coffee surface. Pull back to cup. Final typography collapses into the warm opening macro for a loop.

narration.text: What really happens inside your body when you drink coffee?
After you drink it, caffeine is absorbed into your bloodstream.
It travels through your blood and eventually reaches your brain.
Inside your brain, caffeine blocks receptors for a chemical called adenosine.
Adenosine normally helps build sleep pressure.
By blocking its signals, caffeine can make you feel more alert.
But caffeine doesn’t remove the need for sleep.
As your body breaks it down, its effects gradually fade.
So that energy boost? You’re mostly feeling less of your brain’s sleepiness signal.
